clue.text: View of expert opposite

parts.note: a facet is one view or aspect of something
an ace is an expert, someone top of their field

explanation.surface: A specialist gives their opinion from the other side of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'View' seems to give FACE, but it gives a five-letter word and the enumeration (4,2,4) hides a different split.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people sitting face to face are directly opposite each other, an adverbial synonym.

clue.text: Big cheese with FA raised diplomacy

parts.note: taken as written: the Football Association

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: tact is diplomacy in dealing with people

explanation.surface: An important figure finds the Football Association has become more diplomatic.
explanation.definitionFit: A fat cat is a wealthy, powerful person, as is a big cheese: both informal idioms for a bigwig.

clue.text: Neckwear article and stuff, mostly with tax added

indicators.note: mostly means the word loses its last letter, leaving most of it

parts.note: to cram is to stuff
VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax

explanation.surface: A shopper buys a tie and other goods, paying sales tax on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay: it is tempting to read it as A or AN. 'mostly' trims CRAM to CRA.
explanation.definitionFit: A cravat is a scarf-like band worn round the neck, an item of neckwear.

clue.text: Have one of my gifts, and allow me to give you some advice

definitions.meaning: literally accept a tip, a gratuity, that I hand over

definitions.text: allow me to give you some advice
definitions.meaning: the idiom said when offering a piece of guidance

explanation.surface: A generous adviser offers both a present and a word of wisdom.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is both a cash gift and a useful hint, so the phrase works in either sense.

clue.text: Fielder's initial error

definitions.meaning: a cricket fielding position beside the wicketkeeper, and the player there

explanation.surface: A cricketer makes his opening blunder of the match.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the slips are fielders standing in a line next to the wicketkeeper to catch edged balls; first slip is the one nearest him.
explanation.definitionFit: Slip means a small mistake, and first means initial, so the cricket term doubles as an opening error.

clue.text: Caught up with papers showing Roman god

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
ID, identity papers

explanation.surface: Someone caught up reading the papers finds a story about a Roman deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupid is the Roman god of love, counterpart of the Greek Eros.

clue.text: Catalogue Hungarian composer for the listener

indicators.note: for the listener means the word is to be judged by how it is heard; the run of letters inside listener is a coincidence, not a hidden word

parts.note: Franz Liszt, the Hungarian pianist and composer

explanation.surface: A record catalogue of a Hungarian composer's works, compiled for music lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: A list is a catalogue, an itemised record of things.

clue.text: Sort of cool when seen differently

parts.note: in means fashionable, cool
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'

indicators.note: differently means the letters of seen are arranged another way

explanation.surface: Something considered cool looks different from another angle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'differently' rearranges SEEN to ENSE; 'when' giving AS is a common crossword equivalence.
explanation.definitionFit: In a sense and sort of are both hedging phrases meaning partly or to some extent.

clue.text: Essay on a theme I, a setter, recollected

indicators.note: recollected, read as re-collected, means the letters are gathered up again in a new order

explanation.surface: A crossword setter remembers writing a themed essay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recollected' looks like memory but is the anagram signal for I, A and SETTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a formal written discussion of a subject, a long essay on a topic.

clue.text: Town council's pub expert?

parts.note: a local is the pub nearest home, a British usage
an authority is an expert on a subject

explanation.surface: A council employs a specialist in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the local' is your nearby pub; 'council's' reads as 'council is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A local authority is the body running local government, such as a town council.

clue.text: Follow railway line

explanation.surface: An instruction to walk alongside the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Track means both pursuing something's trail and the rails of a railway.

clue.text: Villain in favour of splitting money returned

indicators.note: splitting means the second piece goes into the middle of the first, dividing it

parts.note: a rebate is money paid back
pro means in favour of

explanation.surface: A criminal backs a scheme to share out refunded cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splitting' tells the solver the longer word is broken open by the shorter one.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is an unprincipled person, a rogue or scoundrel.

clue.text: Resolute, a worker perhaps crossing weir

indicators.note: crossing means the outer pieces span the other, holding it between them

parts.note: an ant is a worker, as in worker ants
a dam, like a weir, holds back a river

explanation.surface: A determined labourer wades across a weir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' has the article and insect straddle the barrier; 'perhaps' flags the insect as one example of a worker.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant means refusing to be swayed, firmly determined.

clue.text: 'Beer' in concise dictionary in 'local' language?

indicators.note: in means one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: dict is the short form of dictionary, so a concise dictionary
ale is a beer

explanation.surface: A short dictionary entry for a word for beer in regional speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concise' belongs to the abbreviation leaf, and 'in' places the drink inside; the quotes around 'local' hint at regional speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect is the form of a language spoken in one region, a local speech.

clue.text: Binoculars, range good, taken by young women

parts.note: a field is a range, as in field of vision
lasses are young women

explanation.surface: Some girls are handed binoculars that work at long range.
explanation.definitionFit: Field glasses are binoculars, used outdoors for distant viewing.

clue.text: American soldier arresting a coarse Italian patriot

indicators.note: arresting means the outer piece captures and holds the inner

parts.note: GI is a US soldier
ribald means coarse, vulgar

explanation.surface: A US soldier detains a crude Italian nationalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Garibaldi led the fight to unify Italy, a national hero and patriot.

clue.text: Private on short list? That's absolute nonsense

parts.note: a Tommy is a British private soldier

indicators.note: short means the word is cut off before its end

parts.note: a rota is a list of duties

explanation.surface: A soldier dismisses a shortened duty roster as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy, from Tommy Atkins, is slang for a British private soldier; 'short' drops the last letter of ROTA.
explanation.definitionFit: Tommyrot is old-fashioned slang for rubbish or utter nonsense.

clue.text: Tripped, son fell

parts.note: tumbled means fell

explanation.surface: A boy trips and falls over.
explanation.definitionFit: To stumble is to trip and lose one's footing.

clue.text: Depressed, having no strong liquor left?

definitions.meaning: literally run ... such as gin or whisky

explanation.surface: Someone is gloomy because the drinks cabinet is empty.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits means both mood and distilled alcohol, so the phrase covers low mood and an empty bar.

clue.text: Canadian-born US showman, and artist, provides capital

parts.note: Paul Anka, Canadian-born singer and entertainer
RA, Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: An entertainer and a painter put up the money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' reads as money but is the definition: a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Ankara is the capital city of Turkey.

clue.text: Verne novel about eastern front

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the other piece
novel means new, so the letters of the word take a new order

explanation.surface: A Jules Verne novel set on the Eastern Front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges VERNE to VENER, and 'about' puts E inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin surface layer, a front that hides what is beneath.

clue.text: Huge insect on mother, beginning to move

parts.note: ma is mother

indicators.note: beginning to means only the first letter of the next word

parts.note: a moth is an insect

explanation.surface: A big bug lands on mum, who starts to stir.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means after, so the insect comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Mammoth as an adjective means enormous, from the vast prehistoric elephant.

clue.text: Monster in bibliography — Dracula?

indicators.note: in means the answer is found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Is a monster listed in the reading list for Dracula?
explanation.definitionFit: The Hydra was the many-headed serpent of Greek myth killed by Heracles.

clue.text: Have in French cheese, and cake

indicators.note: in means one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: Brie is a French cheese
to own is to have

explanation.surface: A shopper takes some brie and a slice of cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A brownie is a small square of dense chocolate cake.

clue.text: Sit next to character, one worthy of imitation

parts.note: a role is a character in a play
to model is to sit for an artist

explanation.surface: Sitting beside a person whose example is worth copying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'next to' simply joins the two pieces; 'Sit' is the verb an artist's model does.
explanation.definitionFit: A role model is a person others look up to and copy.

clue.text: Silly how picture ends?

parts.note: the question how is answered by 'in an', the way the word ends

indicators.note: ends means the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A daft question about the way a film finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as IN AN E: the word picture ends in an E.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means pointless and foolish.

clue.text: Fuss excessively around daughter

indicators.note: around means the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: too means excessively

explanation.surface: A parent makes an excessive fuss over a daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A to-do is a commotion or fuss.

clue.text: A tiny criminal in very fine novel

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters go inside the other pieces

parts.note: fair weather is fine

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent, so the letters are twisted round

explanation.surface: A small offender appears in a superb book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' is the definition, not an anagram signal; 'criminal' rearranges A TINY to ANITY, and 'in' puts it within the very-fine pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanity Fair is the novel by William Makepeace Thackeray.
